Write a critique on a chart in a published work (book/article/news website).



Chart of Total Welfare Spending


This graph is supposed to depict the welfare spending per day and per hour on every household in poverty. This graph was used in a political argument by Republican senator Jeff Sessions. There are several reasons why this graph is misleading and doesn’t serve as an accurate visualization of the data.
Firstly, the chart excludes a large amount of context; there is no visible information about what types of welfare programs are being included or excluded from these statistics. The news article states that when doing the calculations for this chart, Sessions and his team included a wide variety of programs, including Medicaid, food stamps, and several other means-tested programs aimed at those with low incomes; he even includes health benefits given through an employer. The calculations also did not take into account the fact that many individuals who are not in poverty also benefit from these programs, but they are not included in the data shown in the chart. By not strictly defining what constitutes a welfare program and by not including a significant portion of welfare recipients in these data, Sessions has inflated the figure of $168 per day of welfare spending for those in poverty. Another issue is the fact that the chart is also comparing the welfare spending to median income; however, the median income does not include health benefits given by an employer, while Sessions’ calculation of the welfare spending does factor in those health benefits. This is an inaccurate and misleading comparison, especially given the argument Sessions is making and the way the chart is constructed to show the two amounts side by side.
In addition, the chart only shows these two dollar amounts - welfare spending per day and per hour, as compared to the median income per day and per hour. All parts of the chart, including axes, labels, and the graphed data as well, are very elementary and basic. Even the subtitle includes the inaccurate comparison to median income.
While the chart is simple to look at, it doesn’t convey anything meaningful; we don’t know what is considered a welfare program for these data, we don’t know from which or from how many individuals this data was gathered, and we don’t know when this data was collected. Readers can not trust the message that this graph is presenting without having access to the full context of the data. Considering all of these factors, we can assert that this chart is misleading and doesn’t effectively visually represent the data.

In the navigation bar, I included a tab for a bio page, as well as a page for my updated resume, so that visitors can learn more about me and my skills and experience for the purposes of professional growth and opportunities. Additionally, I’ve added tabs for classes in which I have used R and extensive data visualization and analysis; each class tab has a dropdown menu that connects to various assignments and other content. Overall, I believe that this website is a valuable and compelling way in which to showcase my work and data analysis skills, and I plan to continue updating it to serve as a meaninful portfolio as I grow in my career.

title: Literature & Media Reviews
text:
“Dataframed” is a podcast hosted by DataCamp featuring renowned data scientists’ insights of latest data science developments. Pick one recent podcast epidsode, listen, and write a one-page review.

I listened to the DataCamp episode titled “#298 Data Storytelling Skills to Increase Your Impact with Kat Green”. In this episode, Kat Green discusses the valuable skill that is data storytelling and why it is important for data to tell a story in order to be communicated in the most impactful way.


A key point that she makes is that it’s crucial to know your audience and how they will best receive the data; for example, you will have to take different approaches to your data storytelling depending on whether you’re presenting to your colleagues at work, your friends and family, the new person who just started at the company you work at, or the general public. Her approach is to always start with the big picture of your story or the main message you want to get across - then, based on your audience, you can add in more technical detail as needed. For instance, you can include a large amount of tecnical detail and jargon if you’re presenting to your team of coworkers, but if you’re presenting to a wider audience made up of the general public, it’s best to avoid jargon and technical terms and to make the message easy to digest for a broad spectrum of people. Green herself uses what is called the “3 Act Framework” - what she also calls the “And, What, Therefore” framework. The first act “And” gives background and context to the problem or issue you are describing and explains why it’s important or relevant. The second act “What” explains what the root of the problem or question is that you want to examine and the methods you will use to do so. The final act “Therefore” is when you give solutions to the problem and drive your argument home with final conclusions.


Green also advocates for practicing storytelling often in order to build and improve this skill. She claims that she herself starts all her data stories in written form in order to have clarity in what her story is trying to achieve. When the host asks her what role dashboards play in data storytelling, Green states that dashboards, in her view, are for those who already understand and are very familiar with the data, so it doesn’t have the same impact as data storytelling, which aims to reach a broader audience.
